questions.q: In this lesson, what is a "contract" between two pieces of code?
questions.explain: Bugs like "payment of ₦undefined" happen when the publisher and the listener each have their own idea of the payload. Writing the contract as one type lets the compiler check both sides.
options: A legal agreement with the payment provider
The shape and meaning of data one piece hands to another (an id, an event payload, a command result), which should be written once as a type and checked everywhere it is used

questions.q: Why did placeOrder("u-ada", "prd_pro-monthly") compile when the parameters were (productId: string, userId: string)?
questions.explain: Structural typing only sees "string". A brand (Brand<string, "ProductId">) gives each kind of id a different type that exists only at compile time.
options: TypeScript does not check function arguments
TypeScript compares types by structure, and both ids are plain strings, so any string fits either parameter
The strings were too short to check

questions.q: Branded ids exist only for the compiler. What does this print?
questions.explain: The __brand property is a fiction for the type checker. At runtime the id is the same string, so brands cost nothing and serialise normally.

questions.q: Why store money as a branded whole number of kobo instead of a number of naira?
questions.explain: Whole kobo are exact integers. The brand adds a second guarantee: an amount only exists if it went through the checked kobo() function.
options: Floats cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly (3 × 1.1 is 3.3000000000000003), and the brand stops plain numbers and naira values from being passed where kobo are expected

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1.1 has no exact binary representation, so the product is slightly off and a payment of exactly 3.3 does not match. Integer kobo have no such problem.

questions.q: In the lesson, where is value as ProductId allowed to appear?
questions.explain: An as is a promise the compiler cannot verify. Keeping the only one behind a check turns the type ProductId into "a value that was checked", everywhere else in the code.
options: Anywhere a string needs to be passed as a product id
Only inside the parse function, right after the check that makes it true

questions.q: What does this kobo() helper return or throw?
questions.explain: Only whole, non-negative safe integers pass. Zero is a valid amount (a free plan); a fraction or a negative number is refused where it enters.
options:
ok 500000
Not an amount in kobo: 3.3
Not an amount in kobo: -100
ok 0

ok 500000
ok 3
Not an amount in kobo: -100
ok 0

ok 500000
Not an amount in kobo: 3.3
Not an amount in kobo: -100
Not an amount in kobo: 0

questions.q: Why model an order as PendingOrder | PaidOrder | CancelledOrder instead of one interface with optional paidAt? and reason? fields?
questions.explain: With optional fields every combination is allowed, including "paid without paidAt". A discriminated union lists only the legal states, and status tells TypeScript which one you have.
options: Each state has exactly its own fields, a status typo is impossible, and a transition like markPaid can require a PendingOrder, so paying a paid order does not compile
Because JSON cannot store optional fields

questions.q: In RecordPayment, why does markPaid(order, …) compile only after if (order.status !== "pending") throw …?
questions.explain: Narrowing is how the runtime check and the type meet: the if proves the state, and the compiler remembers the proof for the rest of the block.
options: Before the check order is an Order (any state); after it, TypeScript has narrowed it to PendingOrder, the type markPaid requires

questions.q: A new status reaches label at runtime through data the compiler never saw. What happens?
questions.explain: assertNever gives you a compile error while a state is unhandled in your types, and a loud runtime error if an unexpected value slips in anyway, here through an unchecked as on parsed JSON.

questions.q: What does const badge: Record<Order["status"], string> = { … } give you when a new status is added?
questions.explain: A Record over a union of literals is a lookup table the compiler checks for completeness, a lighter alternative to a switch with assertNever.
options: A compile error until the new status has a badge, because the record needs a key for every member of the union
A runtime error on the first request
The new status gets a default badge

questions.q: Why is type PlaceOrderBody = Infer<typeof PlaceOrderBody> better than writing the DTO interface by hand?
questions.explain: A hand-written interface and a schema are two sources of truth that drift apart. With Infer, changing the schema changes the type, and every use is re-checked.
options: The type is derived from the schema that checks the data at runtime, so the two can never disagree
Interfaces are not allowed in contract files

questions.q: What does the strict body schema do with an extra total field?
questions.explain: A client must not choose its own price. The strict schema refuses unknown keys with a 400, so the attempt is visible instead of silently dropped.

questions.q: The DTO has productId: string, the command request has productId: ProductId. What happens between them?
questions.explain: The route is the boundary. A schema checks the shape; a parse function checks the meaning and produces the branded type the rest of the module relies on.
options: The route calls parseProductId, which checks the string and brands it, so handlers only ever receive checked ids

questions.q: What does as const satisfies Record<BillingErrorCode, number> on the status table do?
questions.explain: An annotation would widen the values to number; satisfies checks without widening, and as const keeps the literals.
options: It converts every status to a string
It checks that every error code has a numeric status (a missing code is a compile error) while keeping each exact literal, so BILLING_STATUS.AMOUNT_MISMATCH has type 422
It makes the table editable at runtime
It is the same as a type annotation

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: as const makes the object readonly for the compiler only; at runtime it is an ordinary, unfrozen object. Use Object.freeze as well when runtime immutability matters.

questions.q: What does this custom error carry?
questions.explain: The status comes from the checked table, the name is set from the class, and reason is a typed union that client code can switch on exhaustively.

questions.q: Why are BillingCommands and the payload types written as type aliases rather than interfaces?
questions.explain: An object type alias is assignable to Record<string, unknown>; an interface is not, since it could be extended with more properties later. It is a small rule that saves a confusing error.
options: Helpers such as CommandOf in @zudojs/cqrs and EventUnion in @zudojs/events require Record<string, unknown>, which an interface does not satisfy because it has no index signature
Type aliases are faster at runtime

questions.q: The raw @zudojs/cqrs bus takes the result type as a type argument. What does this print?
questions.explain: The number in execute<PlaceOrder, number> is a claim nothing checks, so TypeScript believes claimed is a number while it is an object. The lesson's typed layer takes the result type from the command map instead.

questions.q: What does the lesson's Handlers<BillingCommands> mapped type turn into a compile error that the raw bus only reports at runtime?
questions.explain: A mapped type over the command map has one required key per command. Leave one out, or return the wrong result, and the handler table does not compile.
options: A command in the map without a handler (the raw bus throws CommandHandlerNotFoundError when it is executed)

questions.q: This is a miniature of the lesson's typed layer. What does it print?
questions.explain: "prd_pro" has 7 characters. send's name chooses both the request type and the result type from the map, and the raw bus still does the routing at runtime.

questions.q: With raw @zudojs/events, bus.on<Event<OrderPaid>>("stock.low", handler) compiles. Why, and what does the lesson's typedEvents change?
questions.explain: A bus whose names are runtime strings (so wildcards and plugins work) cannot know every payload. A thin layer over a type-level map restores the connection without giving up the runtime features.
options: The type argument is not connected to the name, so it is only a claim; typedEvents<BillingEvents> takes the payload type from the map entry for the name you pass
The bus checks payloads at runtime

questions.q: What does this typed event layer print?
questions.explain: Each publish reaches only the handlers for its name, so the order.paid publish ran one handler. Inside the handler, event.payload.total is typed from the map; reading event.payload.amount would not compile.

questions.q: Why do the handlers depend on OrderRepository (an interface) instead of MemoryOrders or a PostgreSQL class?
questions.explain: A port says what the handler needs, not how it is done. The token for the port is what ties a concrete implementation to it at one place.
options: So the handlers work unchanged with the in-memory store in tests and the database in production; only the composition root decides which one is used
Classes cannot be imported into handlers
Because the container only accepts interfaces

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: createToken<Clock> makes resolve(CLOCK) return a Clock. Every createToken call makes a new, unique token, even with the same name, which is why the lesson creates all tokens once in ports.ts.

questions.q: What does registerFactory(TOKEN, (orders, clock) => …, [ORDERS, CLOCK]) check at compile time?
questions.explain: Whether each token is registered is still a runtime question. registerClass with an inject option is not checked against the constructor, which is why the lesson uses factories.
options: Nothing; the inject list is only used at runtime
The factory's parameter types come from the tokens in the inject list, in order, so tokens in the wrong order or of the wrong type are a compile error
That the factory is only called once

questions.q: Environment values are strings. What does this config schema produce?
questions.explain: coerce turns the string into a number, and int() refuses a fraction, so a price with kobo in the wrong unit stops the app at start-up. Infer then types the config for the code that reads it.
options:
{ currency: 'NGN', pro_plan_price: 500000 }
[ 'pro_plan_price: Cannot coerce string to number' ]

questions.q: What is the composition root in the billing module?
questions.explain: One place builds everything. Swapping the clock for the real one, or the memory stores for PostgreSQL, changes only this function.
options: createBillingContainer: the one function that chooses implementations for every port and wires the buses, so no handler builds its own dependencies

questions.q: The provider sends the same "charge.success" webhook twice. What does RecordPayment do the second time, and why?
questions.explain: Providers retry until they get a success. Answering a genuine retry with an error would make them retry forever; a different payment for the same paid order is still refused with 409.
options: Throws ORDER_NOT_PENDING, because the order is already paid
Returns the already-paid order: the provider reference matches the recorded payment, so a retry is harmless and the provider gets a 200

questions.q: Why does GetOrder answer ORDER_NOT_FOUND (404) when Bola asks for Ada's order, instead of 403?
questions.explain: For resources identified by id, "not found" for anything the caller may not see avoids leaking existence. The rule is enforced in the query handler, where the user id is known.
options: A 403 would confirm the order exists; answering "not found" reveals nothing about other users' orders
Because Bola is not logged in

questions.q: The routes return ApiResult<T>, a union of { ok: true; status: 200 | 201; body: T } and { ok: false; status: number; body: { error } }. What does that prevent?
questions.explain: A union of the two response shapes lets the compiler check each branch of a route, and ok lets callers narrow to the right one.
options: Returning a success without a body of the right type, or an error without a code and message

questions.q: In the lesson's failure() helper, which errors are sent to the client with their own message?
questions.explain: Expected failures (bad input, not found, conflicts) are meant for the client. Anything else is a bug whose message may contain internals, so the client gets a generic message and your logs get the details.
options: Every error, so clients can debug
Only BaseErrors marked expose with a status below 500; everything else becomes a generic 500

questions.q: What happens to a // @ts-expect-error type test when a refactor accidentally makes the line below it compile?
questions.explain: That is what makes it a test: it passes while the error exists and fails when it stops existing.
options: TypeScript reports "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive" as an error, so the build fails and you learn the guarantee disappeared

questions.q: Which statement about types at runtime is true?
questions.explain: Compile-time and runtime checks cover different ground. Every boundary with the outside world needs a runtime check that produces the typed value.
options: TypeScript checks JSON request bodies against their types
Types are erased; data from requests, rows, the environment and messages is unchecked until a schema or parse function checks it
Branded ids are validated automatically when they are created with as
A switch with assertNever cannot fail at runtime

questions.q: order.paid events are stored and replayed by another service. You need to rename total to amount. What is the safe way?
questions.explain: The compiler only sees the code of this build. Stored events and other services are outside it, so a contract that leaves your process must evolve compatibly.
options: Rename the field in BillingEvents; the compiler updates everything
Keep order.paid as it is and publish a new event name (for example order.paid.v2) with the new shape alongside it until every consumer has moved
Change the field and ask consumers to redeploy at the same second
Delete old events from the store

questions.q: In a code review of a typed module, where is an as acceptable?
questions.explain: Every as is a claim the compiler accepts without proof. Keeping them few and next to their proof is what keeps the rest of the types honest.
options: In every repository, to turn rows into entities
In a small number of places, each directly after the check or registration that makes it true, with the reason visible
Never, not even in parse functions

questions.q: Write parseOrderId(value: unknown): OrderId, where OrderId is Brand<string, "OrderId"> from @zudojs/constants. Accept only strings that match /^ord_[0-9a-f]{12}$/; otherwise throw ValidationError("Not an order id") from @zudojs/errors.
questions.explain: The check comes first and the as second, in one function that is the only way to make an OrderId. A ValidationError carries 400, so a route can pass it straight to the client.
questions.expected:
ok ord_000000000001
400 Not an order id
400 Not an order id
400 Not an order id

questions.q: Write formatNaira(kobo) for a whole number of kobo: ₦, the naira with commas every three digits, a dot and two digits of kobo. Do it with integer arithmetic, without dividing into a float for the kobo part.
questions.explain: Math.floor(kobo / 100) gives the naira and kobo % 100 the rest, both exact integers. The regular expression inserts a comma before every group of three digits that is followed only by complete groups.

questions.q: Finish cancel(order: PendingOrder, reason: string): CancelledOrder, then make cancelIfPending(order: Order, reason) call it only for a pending order and return the order unchanged otherwise. Print the resulting statuses.
questions.explain: After if (order.status !== "pending") return order;, TypeScript has narrowed order to PendingOrder, so cancel(order, …) compiles there and nowhere else. Calling it with the paid order would be a compile error.
questions.expected:
ord_1 cancelled Changed my mind
ord_2 paid -

questions.q: Write badge as a Record<Status, string> with grey for pending, green for paid, red for cancelled and blue for refunded, and print the badge of each status in all.
questions.explain: Leave out refunded and the record does not compile. That is the lookup-table form of an exhaustive check.

questions.q: Register a GetOrder handler on a @zudojs/cqrs query bus that returns { id, status } from the orders map, and throw NotFoundError from @zudojs/errors for an unknown id. Execute it for ord_1 and ord_9.
questions.explain: The handler returns a view with named fields, so internalNote stays private, and the NotFoundError comes out of execute unchanged with its 404. Here the result type argument on execute is still a claim; the lesson's typed layer takes it from the query map.
questions.expected:
{ id: 'ord_1', status: 'paid' }
404 Order ord_9 not found

questions.q: Finish failure(error). A BaseError from @zudojs/errors whose expose is true and whose statusCode is below 500 becomes { status, code, message } from the error; anything else becomes { status: 500, code: "ERR_INTERNAL", message: "Something went wrong" }.
questions.explain: The database error's message contains an internal address, which must not reach a client. Only errors designed for clients (expose, a 4xx status) pass through; the rest belong in your logs.

questions.q: Finish a tiny typed event bus over the map Events. on(type, handler) stores the handler under its type; emit(type, payload) calls every handler of that type with the payload and returns how many ran.
questions.explain: The map decides the payload type for each name, so payload.amount or emit("order.paid", { orderId: "ord_1" }) would not compile. The two casts sit inside the bus, where storing handlers of different types in one map makes them unavoidable; callers never see them.
questions.expected:
e-mail: ₦5000 received for ord_1
in-app: ord_1 is paid
2 0

questions.q: Write STATUS for the codes in Code with as const satisfies Record<Code, number>: 404 for ORDER_NOT_FOUND, 409 for ORDER_NOT_PENDING, 422 for AMOUNT_MISMATCH. Then print the status of every code in codes.
questions.explain: Remove a line from the table and satisfies reports the missing code; add a code to the union and the table must follow. The values keep their literal types, so a function can promise to return 404 | 409 | 422.
